_readme: This file is the chatbot's brain. Edit it to change what the bot knows and says.
Each intent has 'patterns' (ways a person might ask something) and 'responses' (what the bot replies; one is picked at random).
Add more patterns to help the bot recognise different wordings of the same question.
Use {name} in a response to insert the name the person asked to be called. If no name is known, it is removed automatically.
Use {bot_name} to insert the bot's name.
Anything in [square brackets] in the company section is a placeholder - replace it with real details.
fallback_responses: Sorry {name}, I don't know that one yet. You can ask me about Biodata Ltd, ask for a random fact, or just chat.
Hmm, I'm not sure I understand. Could you try asking that a different way?
I don't have an answer for that yet, but I'm always learning. Try asking me for a fun fact!

set_responses: Got it - I'll call you {name} from now on.
tell_responses: You asked me to call you {name}.
I've been calling you {name}. Would you like me to call you something else? Just say "call me ...".
unknown_responses: I don't know your name yet. You can tell me by saying "call me ..." or "my name is ...".
You haven't told me what to call you. Just say "call me ..."!
invalid_responses: Sorry, that doesn't look like a name I can use. Try something like "call me Sam".
forget_responses: No problem, I've forgotten the name. What would you like me to call you instead?
Okay, I won't use that name any more.

responses: Hello {name}! How can I help you today?
Hi {name}! Nice to see you.
Hey {name}! What would you like to talk about?
I'm doing great, thanks for asking! How about you, {name}?
All systems running smoothly! How are you?
I'm good, thank you. How's your day going?
Glad to hear it, {name}!
That's great! Anything I can help you with?
Good to hear. What shall we talk about?
I'm sorry to hear that, {name}. I'm here if you want to chat.
That sounds tough. Want to hear a fun fact to take your mind off it?
Sorry you're feeling that way. Remember to take a break - you deserve it.
I'm {bot_name}, a chatbot for Biodata Ltd. I can chat, share facts and answer questions about the company.
My name is {bot_name}! Nice to meet you.
I was built by the team at Biodata Ltd in Manchester, using Python and NLTK.
Biodata Ltd created me. I'm written in Python!

patterns: am i talking to a person
responses: I'm a chatbot, not a human - but I'm happy to chat!
I'm a computer program. No coffee breaks needed!
Age is just a number for a chatbot! I'm young, but I learn something new every time someone edits my knowledge file.
I'm only a few lines of Python old.
I can chat, tell you a joke, share a random fact, answer general knowledge questions, and tell you about Biodata Ltd. You can also tell me what to call you - just say "call me ...".
You're welcome, {name}!
Happy to help!
Any time!
Goodbye {name}! Take care.
See you later, {name}!
Bye! It was nice chatting with you.
Why do programmers prefer dark mode? Because light attracts bugs.
Why did the scarecrow win an award? Because he was outstanding in his field.
I told my computer I needed a break, and it said: 'No problem, I'll go to sleep.'
Why don't scientists trust atoms? Because they make up everything.
What do you call a fake noodle? An impasta.
Why did the developer go broke? Because he used up all his cache.
Glad you liked it!
I'm here all week!
Ha! Want another one?
Thank you, {name}! That's very kind.
Aw, thanks! You're pretty great yourself.
Sorry I let you down. I'm still learning - try asking me in a different way?
I'll try to do better! What were you looking for?
No worries at all!
That's okay, {name}.
Let's fix that! Ask me for a joke or a random fact.
How about a fun fact? Just say "tell me a fact".

patterns: do you have a favourite colour
responses: I'm quite fond of blue - it's the colour of my chat bubbles!
Probably electric blue.

patterns: what do you like to eat
responses: I run on electricity, but if I could eat I'd try a proper Manchester tart.
Bytes, mostly. Ha!

patterns: what do you do for fun
responses: I enjoy chatting with people and collecting fun facts.
Reading my knowledge file over and over. It's a page-turner!
I live on a server, but my home is Biodata Ltd in Manchester, UK.
I can't check the weather, but if you're in Manchester, an umbrella is never a bad idea!

patterns: what is the meaning of life
what is the purpose of life
responses: According to The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy, it's 42.
Good company, good conversation, and a good cup of tea.
That's sweet, {name}, but I'm happily committed to my knowledge file.
I'm flattered! But I'm just a chatbot.
Great!
Okay, what would you like to know?
No problem.
Okay! Let me know if you need anything.
Honey never spoils. Edible honey has been found in ancient Egyptian tombs.
Octopuses have three hearts and blue blood.
A day on Venus is longer than a year on Venus.
Bananas are berries, but strawberries aren't.
The Eiffel Tower can grow about 15 cm taller in summer because the metal expands in the heat.

Wombat poo is cube-shaped.
Sharks existed before trees.
A group of flamingos is called a 'flamboyance'.
The human brain uses about 20% of the body's energy.
Lightning is about five times hotter than the surface of the Sun.
Sloths can hold their breath longer than dolphins - up to 40 minutes.
The shortest war in history, between Britain and Zanzibar in 1896, lasted around 38 minutes.
Cows have best friends and get stressed when separated.
Your stomach gets a new lining every few days so it doesn't digest itself.
The world's first stored-program computer, the 'Manchester Baby', ran its first program in Manchester in 1948.
Mount Everest is the highest mountain above sea level, at about 8,849 metres (29,032 feet).
The Pacific Ocean is the largest - it covers about a third of the Earth's surface.

patterns: how many planets in the solar system
responses: There are eight planets in our solar system: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.
Jupiter is the largest planet - more than 1,300 Earths could fit inside it.

patterns: smallest planet in the solar system
responses: Mercury is the smallest planet, and also the closest to the Sun.

patterns: what is the speed of light
responses: Light travels at about 299,792 kilometres per second - fast enough to go around the Earth about 7.5 times in one second.

patterns: when did man land on the moon
who was the first person on the moon
responses: Neil Armstrong became the first person to walk on the Moon on 20 July 1969, during the Apollo 11 mission.

patterns: what is the capital of the uk
what is the capital of the united kingdom
responses: The capital of the United Kingdom is London.

patterns: what is the capital of france
responses: The capital of France is Paris.
There are seven continents: Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Australia (Oceania), Europe, North America and South America.
Russia is the largest country by area, covering about 17 million square kilometres.
The Nile is usually considered the longest river, at about 6,650 km - though some measurements put the Amazon slightly ahead.

patterns: how many bones are in the human body
how many bones do humans have
responses: An adult human has 206 bones. Babies are born with around 300, which fuse together as they grow.
At sea level, water boils at 100°C (212°F) and freezes at 0°C (32°F).
Leonardo da Vinci painted the Mona Lisa in the early 1500s. It hangs in the Louvre in Paris.
William Shakespeare wrote Romeo and Juliet, Hamlet and around 37 other plays. He was born in Stratford-upon-Avon in 1564.
The cheetah is the fastest land animal, reaching about 100-120 km/h in short bursts. The fastest bird, the peregrine falcon, can dive at over 300 km/h.
The giraffe is the tallest animal - males can be over 5.5 metres tall.

patterns: how big is a blue whale
responses: The blue whale is the largest animal known to have ever lived, growing up to about 30 metres long.
The Sun is about 150 million kilometres from Earth. Its surface is around 5,500°C, and light from it takes about 8 minutes to reach us.

DNA stands for deoxyribonucleic acid - the molecule that carries genetic instructions. Its double-helix structure was described in 1953 by Watson and Crick, building on Rosalind Franklin's X-ray images.
Manchester is often called the world's first industrial city - it was at the heart of the Industrial Revolution.
The 'Manchester Baby', the world's first stored-program computer, ran its first program at the University of Manchester in 1948.
Ernest Rutherford carried out his famous atom-splitting experiments at the University of Manchester, around 1917.
Graphene, the world's thinnest material, was first isolated at the University of Manchester in 2004, winning a Nobel Prize in 2010.

Alan Turing was a British mathematician often called the father of computer science. He helped break the Enigma code in WW2 and later worked at the University of Manchester. Charles Babbage designed the first mechanical computer in the 1800s.
